article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.
article.lede: Our computer workers are investigating how independent systems balance strict instructions with the need to adapt when situations change unexpectedly.
article.lens: We look at how computational systems process complex rules and unexpected changes by reviewing current research papers and technical frameworks.
article.title: Tracing How Intelligent Systems Handle Unexpected Choices and Rules

ABSTRACT
Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated
by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both
step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided
framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations
and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajec-
tory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their
sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally,
DeFA uses step evidence and the steps’ roles in failure propagation to identify the
decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories,
DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment’s
detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis ac-
cess to global execution context. Across Who&When and the Who&When Pro
text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accu-
racy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among
taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video tra-
jectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations
support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the
failure propagation graph. Using DeFA’s diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in
Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6–15 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improve-
ment on subsequent tasks.
1 INTRODUCTION
When an LLM agent fails a task, the final outcome rarely reveals which earlier decision was respon-
sible. Agents interleave reasoning, tool use, and communication (Yao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024),
producing trajectories in which an error and its visible consequences may be separated by many
steps. Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step (Zhang et al.,
2025; Liu et al., 2026), providing specific evidence for debugging and subsequent improvement.
The difficulty lies in tracing how errors arise and propagate through execution to identify the deci-
sive error behind downstream

4.4 TRAJECTORY LENGTH ANDLLMCALLS
Localization gains across trajectory lengths.Figure 2a,b shows exact Step accuracy across tra-
jectory lengths with GLM-5.2. Accuracy generally declines as trajectories grow longer, but DeFA
outperforms the baselines in every length interval on both benchmarks. The largest gains occur at
intermediate lengths: DeFA reaches 45.8% on Who&When trajectories of 11–32 steps, exceeding
the strongest baseline by 12.5 percentage points, and improves accuracy by 18.3 points on Pro tra-
jectories of 6–8 steps (67.6% versus 49.3%). These results show that DeFA’s overall improvement
spans different trajectory lengths. Nevertheless, its accuracy remains only 17.2% in the longest
Who&When interval of 33–130 steps despite leading the baselines, indicating that exact localiza-
tion in long trajectories remains challenging.

5 CONCLUSION ANDLIMITATIONS
We introduced DeFA, which traces agent failures through step dependencies. It combines proto-
col relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory to
capture how steps use earlier information. DeFA then identifies events that may violate task require-
ments and traces their sources and effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Final attribution
uses this connected evidence to compare how steps introduce, transmit, or adopt errors and identify
the decisive error and responsible agent.
Experiments on Who&When and Who&When Pro demonstrate precise attribution gains across
backbones, trajectory lengths, and text and multimodal inputs. Ablations support segmentation,
the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. DeFA’s diagnostic feedback also
improves test accuracy after Trace2Skill skill evolution by an average of 9.0 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can guide skill improvements for subsequent tasks.
Limitations.DeFA’s semantic dependency recovery and failure propagation analysis depend on
the model’s trajectory interpretation; missing or misidentified relations can affect attribution, es-
pecially in long executions with dispersed evidence. Downstream utility has been evaluated for
spreadsheet skill evolution; effectiveness in other domains and forms of agent improvement remains
to be assessed. Future work can improve relation identification in long trajectories and broaden the
applications of diagnostic feedback.

When an LLM agent fails a task, the final outcome rarely reveals which earlier decision was respon-
sible. Agents interleave reasoning, tool use, and communication (Yao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024),
producing trajectories in which an error and its visible consequences may be separated by many
steps. Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step (Zhang et al.,
2025; Liu et al., 2026), providing specific evidence for debugging and subsequent improvement.

4.4 TRAJECTORY LENGTH ANDLLMCALLS
Localization gains across trajectory lengths.Figure 2a,b shows exact Step accuracy across tra-
jectory lengths with GLM-5.2. Accuracy generally declines as trajectories grow longer, but DeFA
outperforms the baselines in every length interval on both benchmarks. The largest gains occur at
intermediate lengths: DeFA reaches 45.8% on Who&When trajectories of 11–32 steps, exceeding
the strongest baseline by 12.5 percentage points, and improves accuracy by 18.3 points on Pro tra-
jectories of 6–8 steps (67.6% versus 49.3%). These results show that DeFA’s overall improvement
spans different trajectory lengths. Nevertheless, its accuracy remains only 17.2% in the longest
Who&When interval of 33–130 steps despite leading the baselines, indicating that exact localiza-

5 CONCLUSION ANDLIMITATIONS
We introduced DeFA, which traces agent failures through step dependencies. It combines proto-
col relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory to
capture how steps use earlier information. DeFA then identifies events that may violate task require-
ments and traces their sources and effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Final attribution
uses this connected evidence to compare how steps introduce, transmit, or adopt errors and identify
the decisive error and responsible agent.
Experiments on Who&When and Who&When Pro demonstrate precise attribution gains across
backbones, trajectory lengths, and text and multimodal inputs. Ablations support segmentation,
the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. DeFA’s diagnostic feedback also
improves test accuracy after Trace2Skill skill evolution by an average of 9.0 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can guide skill improvements for subsequent tasks.
Limitations.DeFA’s semantic dependency recovery and failure propagation analysis depend on
the model’s trajectory interpretation; missing or misidentified relations can affect attribution, es-
pecially in long executions with dispersed evidence. Downstream utility has been evaluated for
spreadsheet skill evolution; effectiveness in other domains and forms of agent improvement remains
to be assessed. Future work can improve relation identification in long trajectories and broaden the
applications of diagnostic feedback.
